subject: zoology
question_text: Compare briefly a centipede and a millipede.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack zoology section (book p.65, SAQ 181). Zoology holds only ONE source book — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no zoology board paper is in the corpus — so the two-book union check and the back-test are both structurally impossible for this card; 'not checked' does NOT mean 'checked and clean'. The mark split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

steps.label: What both are
steps.why: The two animals share every class-level character, so the shared points are written first and the differences after, which is the shape a comparison question is marked in.
common_mistakes: Writing that a centipede breathes by gills. Both groups respire by tracheae.
Giving them a head, thorax and abdomen. The body is a head and a trunk only.
steps.memory_tip: Same phylum, same habitat, same breathing, same excretion — only the legs and the food differ.
steps.margin_note: Shared points first. Four short lines is enough.

steps.label: Centipede
steps.why: One pair of legs on each segment gives a long stride and a fast animal, which suits a group that catches live prey.
common_mistakes: Giving the centipede two pairs of legs per segment. That is the millipede.
Writing that centipedes eat plants. They are carnivorous.
steps.memory_tip: Chilopoda: one pair per segment, poison claws in front, feeds on other animals.
steps.margin_note: Class, legs per segment, poison claws, food, examples. One line each.

steps.label: Millipede
steps.why: Diplo means double, so the name of the class itself records the two pairs of legs on each segment.
common_mistakes: Giving the millipede poison claws. Poison claws are found only in the centipede.
Writing that millipedes are carnivorous. They are herbivorous.
steps.memory_tip: Diplopoda: diplo means double, so two pairs per segment, no poison claws, feeds on plants.
steps.margin_note: The same five points as the centipede, in the same order, so the two columns line up.

steps.label: The key differences
steps.why: Three differences are enough for four marks, and the number of leg pairs is the one that names the two classes, so it is written first.
common_mistakes: Listing only the number of legs. Give the poison claws and the food as well.
Writing the differences as loose sentences. A comparison is marked as a table, one row per point.
steps.memory_tip: Chilo is one pair, Diplo is two pairs. Then claws, then food.
steps.margin_note: If there is room, draw this as a two-column table — the examiner is ticking rows.
